content.thinking:
I'm planning a wizard's bookshelf prop at roughly 2.0m tall, 1.1m wide, and 0.35m deep, styled with cel shading, gold trim, glowing orbs, and candles for a high-fantasy anime look. Since it's a static prop rather than a rigged character, I'm checking whether the builder still requires a root joint even without a skeleton.

I'll create a base root joint at the origin, plus a couple of extra hinge joints for moving parts like a small cabinet door and a hanging sign. For construction I'm sticking to safe primitives — boxes, cylinders, spheres, cones, torus shapes, plus lathe/extrude/sweep operations — and using SVG textures for book spine and rune decals, merging same-colored pieces where possible to keep things efficient.

To manage part count, I'm planning books as painted cover boxes with a cream page block, then layering a separate spine decal plane with transparent background and gold-tinted rune/band artwork so the texture tints correctly without covering the whole box in a repeated pattern.

I'm figuring out the geometry orientation: covers face forward (+Z) showing the spine, while the inset cream page block sits behind, visible as a thin line along the top and back edges between the covers.

For 60 books built from four parts each, that's roughly 240 mesh pieces, so I should look at merging geometry by color group to keep performance reasonable.

I'm wondering how painting interacts with merged geometries that already have UVs—paint baking likely needs an atlas per part, and overlapping UVs from merged boxes could cause chart collisions when different sub-boxes share the same 0..1 space.

Given that risk, maybe books should use flat colour strings rather than cel paint to avoid texel conflicts, reserving paint for larger individual surfaces like shelf frames and planks. With a 64-colour limit, a dozen or so cover colours plus trim should work for distinguishing books.

I need to budget the flat colour palette carefully—tallying book covers, pages, metals, wax, flames, glass, parchment, and ink brings me to roughly 35 colours, leaving headroom while saving paint for wood and other larger surfaces.

For the wooden planks, I'll use a grain-based paint texture with shadow derived automatically from the lit color, oriented along the plank's length. I'll keep the painted area modest to manage texel density, setting paint resolution to 2048 and atlas size to 4096, then move on to laying out the design in real-world measurements.

Now I'm sketching the shelf's proportions: overall width 1.3m and height 2.15m with an arched crown, depth 0.38m, a moulded plinth base, side panels with turned corner columns, and a back panel I'm planning to paint deep indigo with a starfield texture.

I'm working out the shelf layout now: a bottom cabinet section with two doors up to 0.62m, then four open shelf boards at increasing heights up to the 1.9m top board, with the interior width narrowed to 1.18m once the side panel thickness is accounted for. I'm also planning the arched crown pediment with gold trim and a finial on top.

Writing crown polygon points...

Rather than a full gold ring, I'll add a smaller front-facing gold plate carrying a moon-star sigil decal against a dark navy inlay for the crown face, positioning it just in front of the shelf's extruded depth at z=+0.19.

Now I'm working out book and shelf placement: back panel sits around z=-0.18, giving usable depth to about z=0.19, so books of depth 0.24 centered near z=0 put their spines around z=0.12 with slight random forward variation. Checking shelf-to-shelf clearances per bay, I realize the top bay's gap of about 0.105 is too tight, so I need to reassign shelf heights to give proper clearance.

I'm recalculating shelf board centers to get consistent 0.34 spacing, settling on boards around 0.60, 0.94, 1.28, 1.62, and a top board near 1.96, creating a cabinet base plus four interior bays with roughly even clearance for books.

Now I'm sketching the contents of each bay: starting with the lowest bay floor at around 0.6175, planning a row of tall tomes on one side balanced with other objects like stacks, scrolls, or orbs on the other.

For bay 2 I'm settling on books on the left, a scroll rack in the center made from stacked cylinders in a wooden frame with ribboned scroll ends and wax seals, and leaning books plus a small potion bottle on the right. For bay 3, I'm planning a hovering glowing orb with a torus ring above a brass dish in the center, flanked by books, with a candlestick dripping wax on the right and stacked tomes with an open book nearby.

For the open book I'll add it on a small stand with glowing rune pages in bay 3's left side. Bay 4 gets a candelabra with a row of candles, scrolls on top of books, an armillary sphere with gold torus rings on a stand for that iconic wizard look, and a crystal cluster with glowing cones on the left. The crown top of the shelf will hold candelabras with three candles each side plus stacked books and a rolled scroll, and the cabinet needs two doors with hinge joints and gold trim.

I'm skipping the hanging lantern idea since it complicates the bounding box, and keeping decorative extras modest rather than adding complex hanging banners or tassels. For the base, I'll scatter a stack of books with a candle puddle on the right, leaning scrolls on the left, and a tall candlestick with wax drips as a floor prop grouping around the shelf's foundation.

Now I'm settling on the paint colors — warm walnut-brown wood tones with horizontal and vertical grain variations for the planks, and a darker trim wood for contrast.

For gold accents I want a shaded cel paint rather than flat color for the bigger gold elements, keeping small gold bits as simple flat tones. I'm weighing whether to give books flat colors to save on atlas cost, even though that risks a slight style mismatch against the cel-shaded wood under scene lighting, since they're small enough it probably won't matter much.

Thinking more about painted books, I realize standard BoxGeometry has overlapping UVs across its six faces, so applying a normal-dependent cel paint to a merged or boxed book cover would cause texel conflicts where different faces fight over the same paint evaluation. Since I can't be sure how the bake step resolves overlapping UVs per part, the safer approach is to avoid merging painted geometry for the books and instead treat each book cover as its own simple, non-conflicting surface.

I'll simplify further: use the normal direction to decide paint, with pages visible only on the fore-edge and top/bottom, cream colored, while the spine face carries the cover color and gold banding.

I'm estimating total surface area across all 60 books (roughly 0.17 m² each) to figure out texel density needed for a reasonably sharp texture.

To keep things manageable, I'll simplify the paint logic to a single shared function per book rather than separate paints for board edges and spine detail—using face normal to distinguish spine, cover, and page regions should be enough without overcomplicating the geometry.

I'll keep decal rune glyphs merged by texture variant into four parts placed just above spine surfaces, and for leaning books I'll apply the same rotation matrix to decal geometry before merging so bands and runes stay consistent with each book's tilt, since painted bands key off world-space position anyway.

Defining local coordinates with the spine offset, then deriving the inverse matrix from position and quaternion so I can transform both points and normals back into book-local space for consistent paint application.

For the paint callbacks, I'm planning to use cel-shading helpers that precompute colors by category — spine, gold bands, page edges — so the lookup is a simple map rather than recomputing shading logic each call.

I'm working out face classification by local normal direction: spine faces, board/cover faces on the sides, and top/back faces that mix page edges with cover trim, deciding thresholds like |n.y|>0.6 for top-face pages versus board edges. I'm also listing out several cover color variants — maroon, royal blue, emerald, violet, teal — to vary book appearance.

For glowing elements like orbs or a crystal ball, I'm noting that opaque shells would hide a glowing inner core, so I'm settling on a single glowing sphere with surface texture as the simplest approach rather than layering glass over a glow.

Placing the highlight slightly left of center and upper in the texture to mimic an anime-style shine, accounting for the equirectangular distortion near the poles. For bay 3, I'm planning a floating orb above a brass dish with two thin tilted glowing gold torus rings orbiting it plus tiny glowing motes, building the rings with torus geometry...

Now I'm designing candles: cream wax cylinders with drip details, dark wick cylinders, and lathe-based teardrop flames with a warm glowing outer layer and brighter inner core, plus brass candlestick holders via lathe profiles. I'm also considering whether to add a glow halo card behind each flame but noting the card orientation issue since it needs to face the viewer rather than stand along the up axis.

For scrolls, I'm planning a rolled parchment cylinder lying horizontally with darker spiral end caps, gold rod knobs, a ribbon band, and a wax seal, built as a reusable helper function that assembles the body cylinder and end roll discs with distinct lighter and darker tan tones.

I'm also considering an unrolled scroll draped over a shelf edge or hanging banner, using a textured plane with runes drawn via SVG to simulate painted parchment, placing it as a decorative hanging element on one of the exterior panels.

I'll settle on pinning small parchment notes to the side panels instead — one plane facing +X on the left panel and a mirrored one facing -X on the right panel, each textured with runes and a pin sphere, keeping orientation correct so the text reads upright from the viewing side.

Now I'm sketching an armillary sphere: a lathed foot base, a vertical rod, a few tilted rings made from low-poly torus geometry (equator, meridian, 23°-tilted ecliptic), and a small glowing blue sphere at center for the earth, all in gold with simple segment counts to keep it light.

For the hourglass, I'm planning a frame of two discs and posts holding two opaque cones for the glass, colored a flat pale blue, with the sand kept simple since the opaque glass will hide any interior sand detail anyway.

I could instead paint the single lathe shape with a height-based gradient — sand colour for the lower bulb transitioning to pale glass for the upper bulb, using the point's y-coordinate to blend.

Now I'm sketching out the overall module structure, setting up imports for the geometry builder, math/rng utilities, painting and texture helpers, and the toon/glow shading kits I'll need.

I'm defining the builder instance and planning out the joint hierarchy for the bookshelf, with a base spine joint and hinge joints for the two doors, figuring out positions and orientations before moving into the door panel geometry.

Working out door placement now: the cabinet interior spans roughly ±0.59 in x, so each door is about 0.585 wide, hinged at the outer edges with centers at x=±0.295, sitting near z=0.195 with 0.03 thickness to align flush with the frame's front face.

Vertically the plinth takes up 0..0.12, so the doors run from about y=0.13 to 0.57, matching the cabinet's inner height. I'm planning each door with a raised panel, a gold filigree decal with scrollwork and a star motif, a ring handle with gold boss, gold hinge straps, and a keyhole on one side.

For the filigree I'll use a gold-tinted stroke color for the SVG lines, sized to match the door panel's aspect ratio, then mirror the design for the opposite door by generating a separate flipped texture rather than relying on geometry mirroring.

Writing filigree SVG details...

Generating star field SVG...

Now I'm working out the shelf structure dimensions: a solid backing box behind the starfield texture plane, plus side panel boxes sized and positioned relative to the top board thickness.

Still writing frame geometry...

Still building the column profile...

I'm checking the loop closes properly from axis to axis around the shape, then verifying column placement at the corners doesn't collide with the side walls given their thickness and offsets.

Now I'm designing the plinth as two stacked boxes forming a step moulding, with a thin gold inlay strip along the front edge, then starting on the crown geometry with its own wood extrusion and a smaller front inlay piece.

Writing crown inlay outline...

Working out the crescent moon geometry by finding where two offset circles intersect, solving for the angle using the law of cosines so the inner and outer arcs meet cleanly at the crescent's tips.

I'm working out that the inner arc should trace the portion of the inner circle lying inside the outer circle, passing through its leftmost point, giving a crescent of thickness about 0.04 opening toward the right. The full polygon then combines the outer arc swept from φ through the left side to 360−φ with this inner arc.

I'm positioning this crescent as a gold finial atop the crown apex, extruded thin and facing outward, with its center placed above the apex so its top sits around y=2.54, plus adding a small glowing orb nested in the crescent's opening for extra detail.

Now I'm planning finial posts for the crown's left/right extremes with small lathed urns and glowing cones, then adding a decorative gold rod swept along the crown's upper outline edge to create fringe strands, rounding the corners smoothly as the sweep path follows the outline points.

I realize I need to explicitly bind all non-door geometry to the base bone, since the auto-nearest-joint logic could mistakenly attach parts near the doors to door joints instead — so I'm wrapping part creation in a helper that always passes `bone: base` unless overridden.

For door hinges, I'm placing the joint precisely on the hinge axis at the door's edge with a vertical rotation direction, so door-mounted parts use `bone: door` explicitly while everything else stays anchored to the base, keeping the whole structure resting on the floor plane. Now I'm moving on to writing the function that lays out books across the shelf bays using randomized positions.

Defining book placement logic...

Keeping this generic, for a lying book I set its position at the right edge, floor height plus half the thickness, with a 90° rotation about Z so the spine still faces outward. Since the paint logic uses local coordinates where bands run along the local y-axis of the spine, I need to check how those bands reorient when the book is lying down—they'd appear as vertical stripes instead of horizontal ones.

For a stacked set of lying books, I'm raising each successive book by its thickness along y, adding a small random x offset and a slight yaw rotation around Y to vary spine orientation, composing the quaternions so yaw applies after the base rotation.

Writing paint closure logic...

Still writing spine band thresholds...

Now I'm thinking through adding a central label window on some books, considering a gold label plate with dark ink decal runes drawn on top for decoration.

Decided to make most books (70%) have cream parchment labels with dark purple rune decals, while the rest get bare spines with gold emblem decals instead, using separate texture groups with a few glyph and emblem variants to merge together.

Thinking about simplifying by baking the cream label rectangle and glyph directly into one combined texture rather than layering separate planes, and doing the same for the gold emblem on dark spines.

Positioning the decal planes just off the spine surface, computing geometry per label, merging them into the bone's local transform with a white base color so the texture's own colors show through correctly.

For bigger tomes I want to add gold decorative bits—clasps and corner reinforcements—as a separate merged gold geometry collection per bay, treating this as an optional embellishment on larger flat books.

I realize I don't need a separate pages geometry at all, since the box's top/back faces already get painted cream between the cover edges, so the single painted box handles that illusion fine. I'll skip page-line detail as unnecessary extra complexity, and now focus on how the cover overlay should sit on boards for the larger tomes that are lying flat.

For lying books I need to figure out which face is the "top" cover based on the board normal, then add a gold border frame plus a sigil mark using local board coordinates. I'm sketching cheap distance checks against the edges to decide where border lines go and a radius test around a center point to place a circular emblem with a gold ring and inner dot.

For texture resolution, I'm bumping the border width to around 2 texels so it reads cleanly at my 3mm texel size, and checking the spine decal plane sits flush against the flat spine face.

For book placement, I'm working out how to tilt the last book in the row by rotating it about its bottom corner so it leans naturally against its neighbor without dipping through the floor, adjusting the rotation pivot and offset so the top edge touches correctly.

Now I'm starting to lay out the actual build function, setting up the builder with a paint size and seeding the RNG, then creating the root joint for the whole composition.

Now I'm defining the color palette: gold tones for metal accents, wood grain shades in different axes for the shelf and books, and a navy for variety.

Still writing paint helpers...

Planning the overall structure now: plinth, columns, sides, back, shelves, top board and crown, then cabinet doors, bay contents, top contents, floor props, and finally merged gold details with textured decals. I'm setting up color and position constants for the build before diving into the detailed geometry code.

Still writing shelf board geometry...

Adding more gold rivet studs...

Defining more color palettes...

Writing book builder logic...

Writing spine paint logic...

Still computing board edge distances...

I need to double check the normal orientation handling for lying books, since the local y-axis points in a different world direction depending on how the book is rotated onto its side.

Working through which world-facing side corresponds to which local face for a lying book with spine toward the front: top shows the cover boards, sides show page edges at head/tail, and the fore-edge faces back — that seems geometrically consistent, so I'll leave the clasp detail for lying tomes aside and focus on gold corner caps at the top corners instead.

I'm placing small gold box geometries at the four corners of the book, sized to wrap the board thickness, then applying the book's rotation matrix so they land correctly whether the book is upright or lying flat. I'm also adding a clasp strap across the fore-edge as a thin gold plate, positioned so it reads as a cross-plate on the back edge when the book is lying down.

Now I'm writing the row-placement function that fills a shelf bay from x0 to x1: it randomly generates book thickness, height, depth, and spine offset for each volume, calls the book-creation function with those parameters plus a random cover and optional label, then advances the x position until no more books fit, returning the final x so adjacent rows can continue seamlessly. Next I want to handle color adjacency between neighboring books.

For bay 1, I'm laying out a row of books along the left side, then placing a crystal ball on a small brass tripod stand near the center -- working out the stand height, orb radius, and glow texture so the total height stays under the shelf clearance -- and adding a stack of tomes toward the right side of the bay.

I'm sizing the tome stack carefully: three books of decreasing thickness topped with a short jar candle, trimming the thicknesses down so the stack plus candle fits under the clearance limit, then filling the gap between the ball and stack with upright books ending in one leaning against the stack.

For bay 1, I'm positioning a row of about eight books on the left, the ball with its stand slightly right of center, the tome-and-candle stack further right, and a final cluster of upright books with one leaning piece to finish the row. Then for bay 2 I'm starting a similar left-side book row with a leaning book, followed by a wooden pigeon-hole scroll rack centered in the middle of the shelf.

Now I'm designing the scroll rack's internal structure with dividers forming cubbies, each holding cylindrical scrolls oriented front-to-back with visible circular end caps textured with a spiral parchment pattern, plus a ribbon band wrapped around each scroll body for detail.

To cut down on draw calls, I'm consolidating all flat-colour geometry (parchment, gold, ribbons, wax seals) into merged buffers keyed by colour rather than individual meshes. The tradeoff is that this flat-lit standard material approach loses the painted cel-shaded look other models have, but I'm accepting that inconsistency for now to save complexity.

For the scroll collection, I'm going hybrid: larger hero scrolls (lying flat, unrolled) get individually cel-painted parts, while small background scrolls in cubbies just use the merged flat geometry. Now I'm working out the layout for the second bay — positioning tall leaning books, a lathe-turned potion bottle with glowing liquid, and an hourglass along the x-axis, spacing books on the left, the rack in the center, then the hourglass and a couple of small glowing potion bottles to the right.

For the third bay, I'm designing an open book resting on a lectern stand with tilted glowing-rune pages — two angled page slabs with a semi-transparent glowing rune texture plane hovering just above them — flanked by a few upright books at the far left. In the center of that bay I'm placing a small floating glow orb above a brass dish base with upward prongs.

For the dish and orb assembly, I'm adding gold curving prongs, a scattering of small glowing motes, and two tilted glowing gold torus rings around the sphere for extra shimmer. On the right side I'm adding a row of books plus a brass candlestick with a drip tray, taper candle, and flame, carefully sizing the stack so total height stays under the bay limit.

For Bay 4, I'm starting with a crystal cluster of several hexagonal glowing violet/pink crystal cones sitting on a rocky dodecahedron base at the far left.

Moving along the shelf, I'm placing another row of mixed books, then an armillary sphere centered on the bay with a stand and tilted ring sized to fit height constraints, and finishing with a trio of candles of varying heights on a brass plate, including a thick dripping pillar candle, all with glowing flames.

For the top surface, I'm placing a three-arm brass candelabra with candles on the left, then considering a stack of books with a scroll near the center, but I realize the central crown decoration extends through the full depth of the shelf, so anything placed there would collide with the crown's face -- I need to work out where items can actually sit without intersecting it.

Reworking the crown design: I'm making it shallower in depth and positioning it toward the back of the shelf, which frees up the front portion of the top board for items like candelabras, books, and a globe without any overlap. Writing geometry code...

I'll add a quill resting in an inkwell near x=0.18, shaping the feather as a smoothed leaf-like outline angled upward in white and blue tones.

For the right side, I'm placing a candle on a pillar plus a small stack of books, skipping the globe idea to keep the composition simple. Then for floor props to the right of the plinth, I'm stacking several large tomes lying flat with a melted candle on top.

On the left side at a mirrored position, I'm adding a lathe-turned vase holding rolled scrolls and a staff, with the scroll cylinders tilted and wrapped in ribbons, keeping the overall floor width to roughly 2.3 meters.

Estimating total part count, I land somewhere between 450-550 pieces across structure, doors, books, candles, scrolls, and orbs, with triangle counts comfortably under 60k so performance should stay fine. I'm noting a constraint that lathe outlines need at least three points and must avoid self-touching with x≥0, then starting to write a candle helper function.

Writing candle helper function...

Modeling drips...

Writing flame lathe geometry...

Defining the brass holder lathe profile...

I'll give the holder a gold paint material shared across instances to keep things efficient, then move on to designing the candelabra with a lathed center stem and three sweep arms built from catmull curves.

Placing candles at the arm tips, then moving to the armillary sphere design with torus rings for the equatorial and other bands, rotating them to orient correctly in 3D space.

For the meridian rings I'm positioning them as vertical planes spaced at different rotation angles, then applying an overall tilt to the whole assembly using quaternion multiplication (combining a tilt rotation with each ring's local orientation) rather than stacking Euler rotations directly. I'm also adding the axis rod running through the sphere's center.

Now I'm deciding on ring colors, leaning toward a flat gold material for the thin torus shapes, and sketching an orb helper function that creates a glowing textured sphere for decorative elements.

For the orb texture, I'm designing a 128×64 SVG where only the central 64×64 region maps onto the visible hemisphere, with a radial gradient from bright center to darker rim, subtle swirl paths, scattered stars, and a soft highlight ellipse, while accounting for the vertical compression distortion that occurs near the poles in equirectangular mapping.

Thinking about alternate orb textures too—a cosmic variant with deep blues fading to bright cyan with white star dots and a magenta galaxy swirl, and an ember variant with deep red-orange tones.

I'm parametrizing the orb texture generation so deep, mid, bright, accent colors and a seed can be swapped in easily, with the SVG sized at double resolution for crisp strokes. I'm also sketching geometry for a crystal cluster using cone shapes to form a prism-like body with a pointed tip.

For the crystal glow, I'm balancing emissive strength around 0.6 so facet shading still shows through under the colored glow rather than washing out into flat colors.

Now I'm sketching the rock base as a scaled dodecahedron with a dark stone cel-shaded material, and designing potion bottles with lathed glass bodies holding glowing liquid at lower intensity, plus wooden corks, gold wire rings, and labels.

Also figuring out an hourglass shape via a lathed bulb profile, with sand painted based on vertical position—piled at the bottom, filling partway up, and clear glass elsewhere.

Now I'm designing the frame with top and bottom wooden plates and connecting posts, then moving to scrolls: cylindrical bodies oriented along different axes, painted as parchment with darker end bands made from slightly larger end-cap rings, plus rod knobs at the tips.

Writing the bit helper function...

Still writing merge logic...

Objects like the glowing flames stay unmerged since they need separate materials. I'm using the BufferGeometryUtils import for mergeGeometries, flattening a sphere into a wax seal shape in red, and considering whether to add ribbon tails or a small knotted sphere, plus maybe a hanging scroll element from the top.

I'm tallying up book counts across the bays—roughly 70 total between shelves and stacks—to gauge the paint and bake sizing cost, then moving on to positioning the left and right doors with their hinge offsets along the x-axis.

Still working out door geometry...

For the handle, I'm placing a torus ring hanging from a gold boss sphere near the door's center edge. Then I'm adding hinge straps as small gold boxes along the outer edge with rivets, plus a keyhole plate near the center of the left door.

Now I'm checking whether the door geometry collides with the columns, recalculating door width and hinge position so the edge clears the column radius without overlapping.

I'll trim the door height to about 0.43 spanning 0.13 to 0.56, and add a cabinet back panel plus bottom board to fill the interior behind the closed doors. Then I'm planning gold ornamental details on the outer side panels.

I'm working out the rotation math so the side panel's text reads upright and correctly oriented for a viewer standing at either the +X or -X side, confirming rotation [0,90,0] and [0,-90,0] respectively keep the reading direction consistent.

For the texture itself, I'm planning a gold vine-and-star inlay with a thin gold border on a transparent background, scaled up at 4px per unit for crispness, plus a row of small moon phases rendered as a gold circle with an overlapping darker circle offset to carve out a crescent shape.

I'm also sketching a dark purple rounded plaque behind the door filigree and shelf inlay for contrast, while skipping extras like spiral columns, corbels, and hanging tassels to keep things simple. Now I'm starting to write the starfield generator function.

Writing SVG code...

I'm checking whether the decal's edges stay within the inlay boundary near the corners, since motifs placed too close to the edge would float outside the gold border. I'll shrink the decal to 0.36 wide × 0.26 tall centered at y=0.17 so the motifs stay contained within the central triangle of the inlay shape.

Checking that the medallion radius and flourish positions stay within the inlay bounds at various y-levels, confirming the horizontal vine lines fit properly between the medallion and the edges.

I also need to place the apex moon near the top, then make sure the default export and metadata are set up correctly, importing the Fill type from context for proper typing. Now I'm sketching out helper constants and definitions before writing the actual SVG markup.

Writing box helper functions...

I'm defining a paint function for the columns that applies gold bands at specific ring positions along the shaft, with gold at the base and capital while the rest stays wood-grained.

Now I'm setting the lathe segment count to 10 and painting the plinth moulding with the dark wood texture. For the crown, I'm defining a polygon outline with symmetric points forming a peaked silhouette, plus a scaling helper to resize these points around a center y-value for the extrusion.

Adding gold and navy border layers...

Still placing the gold bead on the crown rim, then adding a small gold pedestal to connect the apex crescent to the crown top.

Still placing orb geometry... total height comes to roughly 2.57 meters, which works. I'm adding lathed finials at the crown sides with small glowing orbs on top.

Switching to the floor stack of books on the right side: six lying tomes stacked with varying thickness, working out the local-to-world coordinate mapping after rotating each book 90° about the z-axis so thickness becomes vertical height, accumulating y position as the stack builds up.

The rotation order applies qz first then qy, and a small yaw shift from the right-end pivot is negligible. For leaning books, positive roll about z tilts the top toward -x, so I'm adjusting the floor y offset to account for the corner dip from the tilt angle.

Now I'm starting the build function with a root joint at the floor origin, and setting up the color palette with gold, parchment, ink, and seal tones for the bookshelf's materials.

Writing paint definitions...

Writing label glyph SVGs...

Still designing emblem variants...

Still writing book geometry...

Adding clasp strap and buckle details...

I'm defining a bits map for tracking colored geometries and a helper for adding transformed bits, plus a decals map for decal geometry. Now I'm writing functions for the candle stick lathe profile and the candle itself with wax cylinder, rim, and drip/flame options...

Adding candle wax drips and wick...

Still writing flame geometry...

Still placing prongs and orb geometry...

Placing the motes along the ring path with a helper to transform local circle points by the ring's orientation. Now I'm designing the open book scene for the left bay: a small wooden pedestal block topped with a tilted lectern slab to hold the book at an angle.

I'm working out the rotation math so the slab tilts back higher than the front, then adding the book itself—a cover box plus two angled page pieces forming a V shape, with a glowing rune plane resting flush against the tilted surface.

Writing placement helper function...

Now I'm working out the open-book geometry in the lectern's local frame, verifying that the 22° tilt quaternion correctly rotates the local forward axis into a front-down direction.

Building out the slab, lip bar, cover, and left/right page blocks with slight rotations so the pages angle outward from the spine...

Working out the rune plane placement and rotation on each page — figuring out the right-angle rotation to lay it flat on the sloped page surface without z-fighting.

I'm adding the two page textures (lines of script on one, a magic circle sigil on the other), then a small dangling ribbon bookmark, a few floating glow motes above the book, and working out the lectern's leg supports as tilted angled blocks.

Adding runes to the book height, then planning the lectern placement in bay 3 and filling the gap with a couple extra books to the left. Now I'm sketching the armillary stand's lathe profile for its foot.

Adding more meridian rings, the ecliptic ring, and a central glow sphere, plus a thin gold axis rod with knobs at each end for the armillary sphere.

Now I'm designing a crystal cluster: a flattened rock base made from a scaled dodecahedron, topped with an array of tilted crystal shards built from merged cylinder-and-cone prisms with varied size, tilt, and glow color.

I'm also laying out other props like potion bottles, a lathed hourglass, and a scroll rack built from framed boxes forming pigeonhole cubbies, each holding a pair of rolled scrolls.

Each scroll gets a ribbon torus wrap and front-facing decal, flush within the rack's 0.2 depth. I'm also sketching out the rack frame itself—seven individually painted wood parts plus gold cornice trim at the top, positioning the rack's center z to align with the scrolls inside.

Now I'm drafting an SVG texture for the scroll end caps: a parchment-colored disc with a spiral swirl pattern rendered using stacked arc paths to suggest a rolled scroll cross-section.

I'm also setting up a stack of lying books as floor props near x=1.0, with varied heights, thicknesses, depths, and slight random yaw angles, spines facing outward, so they read as an ornate toppled pile on the floor.

On top of that stack, I'm adding a thick pillar candle with heavy wax drips and a pool of melted wax at its base, calculating the candle's placement height from the cumulative thickness of the stacked books plus the flame height.

For the left side, I'm shaping a lathed vase with a scrolled profile, giving it a solid hollow-topped form so decorative scrolls appear to emerge from inside, then painting it a blue ceramic tone with a gold band and simple patterned accents.

Now I'm adding five tilted cylindrical scrolls rising from the vase opening, each leaning outward at roughly a 12-degree angle using directional aim vectors so they fan out naturally from the rim.

I'll use the aim function to orient the torus/cylinder quaternions along the scroll direction, applying them to the parts via applyQuaternion for the 15 scroll pieces.
